utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you follow in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Who is just briefly leaving court to do some copying. Good morning, Your Honours. The reason is that we discovered yesterday that there were two newspaper articles from Glas that were referred to events in Bosanski Novi and we did a very quick translation but it's only just arrived this morning. So Ms. Gustin is going to copy it so we can hand out copies and I hope nobody will object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear your objection, Mr. Ackerman. Good morning to you. Appearances for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic. It's impossible for me to form an objection until I see what it is that we are dealing with. Chances are I won't have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good morning to you three. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just ask you a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We talked yesterday about the testimony of that last witness and you suggested I file a motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm wondering if it might be more appropriate to simply make that part of a motion at the end of the Prosecutor's case rather than try to piecemeal issues like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You could do that. But frankly -- I mean I obviously said nothing or very little for a very simple reason that at this particular point in time, it's very difficult to agree with what you said or what you -- because there maybe other witnesses that tie the whole incident up, apart from other considerations, but I obviously wanted to wait for some kind of response from the Prosecution. If you prefer to postpone that, I think at the present time, you're perfectly entitled to do it. You reserve your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As I thought about it last night, Your Honour, I had the same kind of thought you just had that it may not be ripe for decision until we've actually gone through the rest of the Prosecutor's case. I think I'll just postpone it and file later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also because you base your whole argument mainly on the allegation that this was a personal revenge taken by two persons and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was keeping an eye on the television, big mother watching or whatever, and I know Ms. Richterova could have dealt with it on the spot but I think Mr. Ackerman is right in one sense. We could present an argument as to why, the most obvious being that these men were members of the 1st Krajina Corps and no Prosecution was taken and it's part of that part of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is, but one of the documents that you exhibited yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Precisely confirms that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But, Your Honour, I think it's better -- I think Mr. Ackerman in one sense may be right when Your Honour sees the whole aspect of a failure to prosecute that we are going to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will understand, Ms. Korner, that at that point in time, it would have been extremely rash on our part to hint at that, but once Mr. Ackerman himself is hinting at this possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's perfectly appropriate. It's right to say straight away that I'm almost certain that when we get to the end of the Prosecution case, there will be certain matters which are listed in the indictment, for example, in respect of mosques in Banja Luka, which we will be withdrawing some of the details because it's quite clear even at this stage that we haven't established that some of the listed mosques were actually either damaged or destroyed. I do at this stage emphasise damaged. So, Your Honour, I think there will be, as it were, an assessment made by everybody at the end of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's very fair, Ms. Korner. And, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just very quickly, before -- because we have to go into closed session as Your Honour recalls to see about this witness's protective measures, raise two matters? Well, one is entirely, as it were, personal. I hope that Your Honours understand that by my response to Mr. Ackerman's request, I was not suggesting that Dr. Stakic had been denied visits. He does have a family and he has been receiving visits, and I was not by that part of my reply intending to indicate that it was our desire that Mr. Brdjanin should be denied family visits. I was merely pointing out that it's clearly possible for accused who are on trial to receive visits. Your Honour, the second matter is effectively yesterday was the end of the Prijedor evidence with one exception. Your Honours, a witness was called, as I think I mentioned to Your Honour, as part of the Stakic Defence case who inter alia stated that she was present, she was a secretary in Omarska, apparently, when the delegation visited the camp, and that is a matter of extreme dispute. And so it is our intention to call her. We will provide Your Honours and Mr. Ackerman with the transcript of her evidence. We do not, however, intend to tender the transcript. She will merely be called to deal with that aspect of the case. But that will have to be later because we have to make arrangements for her to be brought but otherwise that really concluded yesterday the end of the Prijedor part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's perfect, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, finally on that, we have -- Your Honour may recall I mentioned that because effectively in the way that witnesses have been called, we haven't gone through anything other than a minute quantity of the documents we've produced. We had prepared a schedule of those documents which effectively shows the areas to which these documents relate. That has been given to Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Ackerman -- you haven't had it yet because I'm waiting to see whether Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was checking something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Mr. Ackerman has been asked that he may be given the time that he's away to look at them, and that seems appropriate. It will be my application that Your Honours get a copy of that, but I'll have to wait to see whether Mr. Ackerman objects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While we are at it, perhaps we can take up the matter of Mr. Ackerman's motion and your response regarding the short break asked for. And I asked the Registrar to make a comparative report as to how many times we have sat in 2002, and I think we did extremely well, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 154 days? Not even that actually.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, your microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Martinovic and Naletilic is 109 and Milosevic is 134, and they only started three weeks after we did; Simic is 63; Stakic is 98, although it started in April, but if you add the first three and a half months --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think that's wrong, Your Honour. We had Judge Schomburg remark the other day that that was the 100th day and he hoped it wasn't going to run into 200. So that figure is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Galic, 164. And that -- they started three weeks before we did. Or they were already sitting three weeks before we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I wasn't inviting a comparison I was merely pointing out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I meant to say is we did -- I think we worked a hell of a lot. I think we worked a hell of a lot. That's the conclusion I reach. And considering the kind of case that we have, I wouldn't like to draw comparisons because comparisons are always odious. But the type of case that we have, and the amount of reading that it entails, is indeed time-consuming.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I said it's a matter for Your Honour. I merely pointed out the statistics for this case. If Your Honour is of the view that we are -- that Mr. Ackerman's request should be granted then that's a matter entirely for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I -- leaving apart the family aspect to which we are extremely sensitive, as a matter of right, but we have no reason to believe that there are complaints or that there have been complaints in that area. So we are not attaching to great importance. But the fact that we ourselves are pretty much behind in catching up with the reading that needed to be done with the Prijedor phase, we haven't finished that as yet. So I think we will try to combine everything and our decision is to grant the break, as requested by Mr. Ackerman, with the understanding that there will be absolutely no breaks after that until Easter. That is an understanding. All right? So the figure, I'm told, is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But that's not going to make a difference anyway because our concern is not Stakic or Simic; it's Brdjanin and Talic or Brdjanin. So the witness -- I think we need to go into closed session for a while. So prepare the room please, the courtroom. For the time being, our decision -- this witness initially had not requested any --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he was a Rule 92 witness originally, as you will see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so I don't think the question of protective measures was ever discussed with him because it wasn't intended to call him, so it was only when he arrived here that he made known his concerns. Your Honour, I wonder if the simplest thing would be as I'm aware of his concerns for had me to ask him to deal with it, and then if Your Honours feel there are further questions you need to ask, that perhaps would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course that's perfectly okay with us, provided you don't put the alternative of a closed session as the only reasonable or sensible way of dealing with him or protecting him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the approach should be more or less --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm simply going to ask what his concerns are and why he has them. But, Your Honour, I should point out -- are we in closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Yes, we are in closed session, yes. We are in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can't see it on the screen, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we proceed, sir, look at me. When would you like to return home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but if you really want to return home as soon as possible, I suggest to you to be very brief in your answers because the way we are going, you are going to be here the rest of the week, if not part of next week too. So please try to answer the questions that you are -- that are put to you as briefly as possible. Just answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. Take my advice because otherwise you will be here for days plus the weekend, which is not going to be very nice here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I gather we are promised snow again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, starting from late this evening, I think. Yes, Ms. Korner, he's in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you now about the ethnic composition of Bosanski Novi, and I'm going to show you another map. But first of all, can I put some figures to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm referring to the document which is P60 but I don't think it needs to be shown.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it right that in the census in 1991, the total population of Bosanski Novi was 41.665 occupants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that out of that, the Croats were the tiniest proportion, there were some 403 Croats forming 1 per cent of the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Muslims, Bosniaks, 14.040, 33.7 per cent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'll come -- I know the point you're going to make in a moment but the Serbs, 25.101, so 60.2 per cent of the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then there were some persons who described themselves, and for the purposes of the census, as Yugoslavs, 1.557, forming 3.7 per cent of the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps slightly few more people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, some 564 people who described themselves as "others"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want you please to look at a map of the whole municipality, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And there are copies for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, sir, this is a map that you've had an opportunity to look at before. That shows roughly the makeup of the various villages and areas within the municipality of Bosanski Novi. Would you agree that that is roughly accurate and all it requires for you to say is yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be made, then, P1624?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, within the town of Bosanski Novi itself, were the populations, the nationalities, mixed within that town or were there areas that were specifically Bosniak, specifically Serb, and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the centre of the town, it was rather mixed. There were areas, parts of the town, where the Bosniak population predominated, and other parts where there were more Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, you have our authorisation to be very direct in regard to this part. So you can put it straight to him whether these were Serb, whether these were Croat, whether these were Muslims. Go ahead so that we --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to ask anything more about the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. But if you are, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not because there are going to be other witnesses who are going to deal with the various villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as the area in which you lived, was that a mixed area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was a mixed area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the relationships between the ethnicities, which was nationalities, which was really Serbs and Bosniaks, what were they like before the events of late 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The relations were very harmonious between the ethnic communities, very friendly, and life was good in the town because there were no chauvinistic excesses or perhaps incidents that would be worth mentioning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did that harmonious relationship change really after the first election -- national -- sorry, the first multi-party elections in 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I did notice certain changes, especially after the ethnically-based parties were formed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what changes were those in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A rift began to appear between the young people, I saw also amongst those of more advanced age in sports teams, some guys began to leave, even though they were indispensable. In coffee bars, in pubs, you could begin to feel the division, and places began to appear which were frequented only by people of a specific ethnic origin. That is in one you'd find only Serbs, and in others you'd find only Bosniaks. There were those which were frequented by both but, yes, one could feel a certain tension.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were those tensions affected by what was happening politically? Perhaps I should --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see speeches on television of the politicians, the Serb politicians, Bosnian Serb politicians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I had electricity and when my TV set worked, then yes, I did, but as a matter of fact, no, for the most part, I didn't. I did hear some of the speeches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can we deal first with 1991, after the war in Croatia had started? Was there anything about the speeches that were being made that caused you concern?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what did cause concern was a duel between the Members of Parliament of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, also the concern was exacerbated by certain broadcasts aired by local radio stations in Prijedor and Banja Luka, when I could hear them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were those certain broadcasts which exacerbated the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, more or less, those were speeches and programmes inviting to ethnic humanitarian organisations who were egging people on against other ethnic communities or setting people against other communities. Also, some pieces of information were broadcast which were not based on facts, but I believe it caused concern amongst the Bosniak population, but I'd also say that the Serb population also started to worry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you give us one example of a piece of information which was broadcast and not based on fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was this kind of information, that, for instance, this or that was about to happen, that extremists of another ethnic group would be brought to justice, that they would account, that this or that had to be done, that safety could not be guaranteed in the area, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you directly: Did you ever see Mr. Brdjanin first, physically, in Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never communicated personally with Mr. Brdjanin. I never talked with him. I do not know him except from journals, magazines, photographs and television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you saw in magazines, journals, or television, what was his role? Who was he, as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to my own personal opinion, even though --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman, one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no time frame involved here. I think it needs to be placed within the time frame of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're correct. Ms. Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In addition, that's an awfully broad question to have asked in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, rephrase your question with reference to a time frame, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll certainly do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise I don't agree with Mr. Ackerman that it's broad or too broad.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll certainly rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when did you first become aware of Mr. Brdjanin, if you can give us a time frame?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1992-1993, as we did say that we would not refer to anything that happened afterwards. So it was agreed that we would refer to 1991, that is 1992, in the course of that year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So just to clarify that, did you become aware of him in 1992 or before, in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't be sure about 1991, but I do remember that he was a SDS member in 1992. I think that he had some leading positions but I don't know exactly what his job was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you became aware of him in -- on the television or in newspapers, what were you -- did you become aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a bit difficult to answer that but since he was a member of the SDS, since he held some leading positions there, and since later on, over time, as things progressed, he -- well, it is -- it was my judgement that after all, he was somebody who was consulted and was probably involved in the decision-making processes due to his position within the party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you get that impression? From what you saw in the media or from what people told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I only occasionally saw some programmes from Banja Luka where he was involved. I can't remember a great deal or in any detail. But I do remember that I was pretty horrified by what I heard and it really made me feel uncomfortable. I believe that in one of the speeches, there was a reference to moving the Muslims out of the area, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that -- you said you were pretty horrified. Was that the type of thing that horrified you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if somebody starts planning to move me out of my house or chase me away or arrange for things to happen to me, obviously it would make me feel uncomfortable and I suppose it goes for many other people as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not he ever came to Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know for sure, but I did hear rumours that he did spend sometime in Bosanski Novi. I don't know exactly when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all you heard was rumours? You don't know for sure whether he ever came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, I want to move to the events of 1992. Did there come a time in Bosanski Novi when there were checkpoints being set up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember roughly -- and I know it's a long time ago -- when those checkpoints were set up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think in 1992 -- well, when you say "checkpoints," I suppose you mean places where it was made more difficult to cross over to another area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, yes, can we deal with this in two stages? Were there barriers or barricades, if you wanted to leave Bosanski Novi -- the town of Bosanski Novi and go elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You couldn't do that unless you went through the checkpoints and you had to display certain documents and you were subjected to controls and the documents were issued by the municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was operating the checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the basis of my own experience, I know that there were policemen there, both regular and reserve policemen, and some checkpoints were probably manned by the military, by soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did they start to be established? When did it become difficult to travel out of the town of Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It became more difficult in the course of the second half of 1992. Or perhaps we should say it was risky to travel anywhere at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, within the town of Bosanski Novi itself, were any checkpoints set up in the course of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the town itself, not really, but there were on the outskirts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, then for the next series of questions, can we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Ackerman? Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I know that -- I think it's right that you were not a member of any of the nationalist parties. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I don't think you took a great deal of interest in politics. Is that also right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not during the war but when I was younger, I did take an active role in politics, prior to the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as a result of the 1990 elections, until the events we are going to come to, was there a division of posts in the municipality between the Serbs and the Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was based on a party agreement, and certain posts were held by Muslims, Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you recall a time in around May of 1992, when there was a call, announcements of people having to surrender their weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, unless there is an objection, I'm going to ask you to look at a couple of articles from Glas from that period which you haven't had an opportunity to see in advance. I hear no objection, so could you look, please, first of all, at an article from Glas dated the 6th of May?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are copies available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can see them in Madam Chuqing's hands. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only comment I have is that the translations we were given bear no dates and the originals -- one of them does, the longer one does, but the short one does not have a date, although the paper itself does have a date, so it should reflect the date in the translation it seems to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's right. It's been missed off, but one can see clearly in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman is right and I'm pretty sure that for the time being we can go ahead with what we have with the understanding that they will be replaced as soon as possible with copies that do bear the date of the publication of the issue of the newspaper that they purport to be a translation of.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is there any reason, Your Honour, why the Registrar can't write over the top 6 of May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you are both happy with that, we can do it that way as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honour, this is the 6th of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not 1992. So it's just that -- you may be able to assist on some of the matters that are here, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you find a part in Glas that has something -- it's headed, "Personnel Shifts." Have you found that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's Bosanski Novi and it says that at the most recent session, Mirko Djukanovic from Bosanska Kostajnica has been elected to replace the current SDS assembly president, Radomir Pasic who is also the President of the Bosanski Novi municipal assembly and his deputy will be Drago Djukanovic [sic] from Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm sorry, Your Honour, we now have to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you know anything about the community of municipalities of the Banja Luka region? If you didn't, say so straight away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that article then be made P1625, the date being the 6th of May, 1991?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now can you have a look, please, at a second article which is May 1992. Sir, if you can find an article, say -- that's headed, "Peace, common interest, successful termination of negotiations between the SDS and the SDA regarding the surrender of weapons in Bosanski Novi"? Have you seen that -- have you got that article, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. It's dated May the 7th, and it says, "Today in Bosanski Novi days-long negotiations between the representatives of the SDS and the SDA on the implementation of decisions of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the autonomous region Bosanska Krajina have successfully been brought to an end. This primarily regards the issue of disarming illegally armed groups and individuals who are not part of the regular municipal TO forces. "The meeting was organised by the municipal authorities led by the President of the municipal assembly, Radomir Pasic. The SDS delegation was led by the President of the municipal board, Mirko Dejanovic, and the SDA delegation headed by the President of the city council, Izet Muhamedagic. And the meeting was also headed by the TO Staff Commander and the public security station chief." Now pausing there, sir, at this stage in May of 1992, it looks as though most of the leading positions were held by members of the Serb nationality. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The organisation and collection of weapons has been entrusted primarily to the TO municipal staff and the public security station whereas the political activity aiming at peaceful and casualty completion of the operation is to be carried out by representatives of the SDS and the SDA. And in that sense, Mr. Muhamedagic [Realtime transcript read in error "Mr. Mayhew"] has publicly called for Muslim people who possess illegally-acquired weapons to surrender them in the way that has been previously agreed upon. And Mako Dejanovic has sent a similar call to Serbs who illegally possess weapons. "Official authorities and legal armed formations have duty to provide security to citizens who surrender their weapons. Concurrently with the activities on the surrender of weapons, Muslims shall be joining the TO and the public security station for the purpose of creating a structure along ethnic lines that is to mirror the ethnic composition in the municipality." Now, sir, is that what you were referring to when you told us a little time ago that the leader of the SDA called for the Muslim people to surrender illegal weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that the calls came from the municipality but I know myself that on the radio, there were calls being issued by the President, not of the municipal SDA but the regional SDA, Mr. Muhamedagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 36, line 10, Mr. Mayhew has reappeared, and I'm quite certain that was not what was asked. Maybe it needs to be cleaned up now while somebody might remember what Ms. Korner asked there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I read out -- I tried to pronounce the gentleman's name, but I'll spell it out so we don't have any problem. It's M-u-h-a-m-e-d-a-g-i-c with an accent. And I have real difficulties with that name, as everybody can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Mayhew will be very much flattered knowing that he is being confused with this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in actual fact, this was a call for the surrender by all parties of illegally-held weapons. I want you to have a look, please, at a further document which is Exhibit P1652.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's in the Bosanski Novi binder which I hope Your Honours have with you today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, no exhibit number has been assigned to this second newspaper article yet and should be done now for record purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That would be 1626, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It would, thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Always alert to the transcript. This is a document dated the 15th of May. It's in the binders, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but we don't have it here ready with us because it was not included in the list that was indicated to us. So our secretaries did not --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I did say, Your Honour, as we only had one binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's no problem, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a document from Bosanska Kostajnica branch police station and when we saw it on the map we saw it was right up in the corner of the municipality of Bosanski Novi. Which says, "On the 15th of May, 1992, a thorough search of Muslim houses in the Uzice neighbourhood began. The search much was carried out by policemen from the special purposes unit. And during the search, many mistakes that cannot be tolerated were observed; arrogant behaviour, seizure of weapons for which citizens possessed valid licences, no record was made of weapons and equipment seized. It was noticed that pistols and other equipment were not handed over to the police station but were appropriated. "We are of the opinion that this kind of behaviour damaged the reputation of police officers because it was also citizens of Serbian nationality who drew our attention to these omissions. Any cooperation with this kind of unit [group] is impossible. Station commander Marinko Curcija." Can you pronounce that last name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Marinko Curcija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's dated Bosanska Kostajnica the 15th of May, 1992. First, do you know -- did you know this man, Marinko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was he when you knew him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was at the branch police station in Kostajnica. That is when I knew him, but I think that later on he also became the chief of the security service in Bosanski Novi. I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, this document refers to policemen from special purposes unit. Do you know anything or did you know anything about that unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't, but this document I deem that they existed because later on, from those who lived in the locality of Urije where this happened, I heard that those groups behaved as they pleased.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The complaint was that weapons were being seized from Muslims even though they had valid licences. Was that something that you became aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Everything that could be used to fire from was being seized, even when people showed legal documents, that is their licences for hunting rifles or hunting carbines, all of that was seized, and they were issued no receipts or anything, at least that is what people who lived in Uzice in Bosanska Kostajnica said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you hear this from people in other areas as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that it was being done in the Japra valley, in suburban locality Urije where nobody asked, "Do you have your licence for the possession of a weapon?" They were just seized and no receipts were issued for the weapons seized.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the same thing happening to Serbs who had valid licences? In other words, were their weapons being seized?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am quite sure that weapons which were brought to the municipality, the municipal services refused to take them over so that those people had to take them back. I am not aware of the seizure of weapons in Serb localities, although the proclamation requesting people to hand over their weapons was an all-embracing one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you become aware of weapons being supplied to Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1992, Bosanski Novi was overflown by both planes and helicopters. I know that helicopters used to go to some boundary areas of Bosanski Novi and some areas inhabited by Serbs only. So all I know is that they flew over and landed but what they were transporting I could not see that nor was it accessible to me. But according to information, they were bringing in weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want you to look, please, at another document which is Exhibit P1653.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this comes from the CSB in Banja Luka. So it's a Serb report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's headed "Review of security relevant information for Bosanski Novi municipality." It doesn't, I don't think, have a date on it. But it says that, "The political and economic situation in the country, which has been deteriorating for several months now, is reflected in almost all aspects of life, and in the security situation in this area. In view of its geographic and strategic position, Bosanski Novi has become interesting to all of the warring parties, i.e., wartime and ideological opponents. The extremist part of the SDA has proceeded to issue arms on a massive scale to citizens of Muslim ethnicity prepared primarily to execute any tasks entrusted to them by the SDA." Now, were you aware of any massive arming or the issuing of arms on a massive scale to citizens of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a nutshell, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is suggested in the third paragraph that a meeting was held in Blagaj on the 9th of May, 1991, which prepared a plan for the liquidation of Serbs in that municipality. Now, first, do you know of any such meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether it took place in Blagaj, I don't know. But there were meetings around areas, the SDS held its meetings in various villages, and I suppose that the SDA must have also held its meetings in various areas, especially in the upper valley which is almost exclusively Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The suggestion is that at one of these meetings, there was a plan made by the SDA to liquidate Serbs in that municipality. In your view, what was the likelihood of Muslims being able to liquidate Serbs in the municipality of Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think they would. Even if they wanted to, I don't think they would have been up to doing it, because the correlation of forces was in favour of the Serbs. I mean the Serbs were more numerous, and also had more weaponry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then if we go to the very last part of this document, it states that "Citizens of Serbian ethnicity are organised within the system of TO, mainly through the efforts of Radomir Pasic, president of the Bosanski Novi municipal assembly. So far, about 1.300 Serbs have been armed, mostly are automatic infantry weapons and they control a considerable amount of equipment for -- and what's translated as anti-armour combat -- 90-millimetre launchers, one 6 -- 76-millimetre howitzer gun and a smaller amount of 82- and 120-millimetre mortars." Now, as far as the makeup of the TO was concerned, was that, as is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. suggested here, a mainly Serb organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was mono-ethnic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by mono-ethnic, you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbs, that the Serbs held the Territorial Defence. Secondly, I don't think that this is an accurate figure, because if we are talking about the period of time, I don't know, because you didn't tell me. But it must be 1992, I think there were more weapons there and that hardly a single man of Serb ethnicity who was able-bodied didn't have a weapon if he wanted to have one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You can put that document away now. Now, sir, finally before we reach the events of June of 1992, had any dismissals of non-Serbs taken place before the violence began in Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Sporadically. Individuals. But after the power was taken over, then the dismissals began on a large scale, and I was an eyewitness to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll deal with that, then, at the point at which we reach it. Two matters finally, then. Before what you describe as the takeover of power, had there been any, as it were, isolated incidents of violence, bombings, anything like that, within the town of Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both in Novi and around it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was -- were any particular types of -- let's deal with explosions. Were any types of buildings targeted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the early days, old buildings, old Bosnian houses, which unequivocally belonged to Muslims. I mean in terms of architecture, they were indubitably Muslim, but I do not think there were any casualties at the time of those minings because a warning would come that something would happen and people would seek shelter. Then grenades were also thrown into various commercial business outlets belonging to Muslims, coffee shops, shops, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There -- were there any incidents where people were beaten or anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe there were such instances but people who were not in mortal peril did not come to seek help, because that was too dangerous because they had been threatened that they were not to go and seek help or else, if they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. This is the final question. Then we'll come to the events. When did you first hear of the organisation calling itself the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think as soon as power was taken over, although I think that the Crisis Staff had been put into place even before that. It had its premises in the municipal hall [redacted] [redacted], I knew those people who were on the Crisis Staff, at least some of them or some of them more, some of them less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pause for a moment, sir. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, can we please redact that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we need to redact the answer from line 43 -- line from 43 after the words "municipal hall" redact all the other words until we start again with the two words, "I knew those people." All right? Did you follow me?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think we perhaps need to go out of an abundance of caution into private session because I want to follow up on what he said there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this really is the final question about the events before the takeover. Did you become aware of more armed persons within Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In camouflage uniforms and under arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these appear to be members of the regular military forces, either the army or the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think those were groups which were not under the control of lawful authorities, but these authorities never tried to stop them from moving around the town, carrying their weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what made you think that these were groups not under the control of lawful authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It transpired later on that those were trouble-makers, even after the takeover of power, and the authorities then tried to -- had show-downs with those groups in the town and because there were murders and some of those groups were decimated. Those groups later on became known as "Suha Rebra," dry ribs, and something else. I don't know. But at any rate, there was another group, and the security service of the municipal assembly later on settled scores with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's always the same thing. One other matter I need to ask you about. Were you aware of the presence of the UN forces just across the river in Croatia? UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was. Those forces were stationed near the bus terminal in the neighbouring Brod [as interpreted] [redacted] [redacted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can just answer this one yes or no. Were you ever made aware of meetings at the end of May between Mr. Pasic and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just for accuracy, Your Honour, page 45, line 25, it's not Brod, it's Dvor, D-v-o-r.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I'm afraid it's happened again, which I hadn't picked up, in line -- I need to have redacted lines 23 to 25. On page 45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Yes. I think that ought to be redacted. Lines 24, after the word, "I was" after the word, "Bus terminal," redact the other words, the next four words, five, six, seven, next -- redact all the words before the word "could be -- could be seen." Right until the very end, okay? All the words after "bus terminal" up to the full stop. All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll just ask, Your Honour, that may be an appropriate question -- time to break. I'll just ask the question I was asking when Mr. Ackerman pointed that out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever aware of meetings between Mr. Pasic or a meeting between Mr. Pasic and representatives of the UN at the end of May in respect of people wanting to leave Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did hear about it, and on one occasion, I also talked with Mr. Balija, who was an educator, and heard that there were meetings between the representatives of the Bosanski Novi municipal assembly and the international organisation, but I do not know where or when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this may seem a question to which the answer is obvious sir, but why, as we'll hear, were Bosniaks so anxious to leave were Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're asking me about the time prior to the takeover or after it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the takeover. We'll come to what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A sizeable part of the citizens had analysed the situation and perhaps even foresaw what would happen, and therefore tried to leave the area, their homes, and their houses. Those who wanted to do that prior to the takeover, perhaps also had certain reasons, because some swapped their property, but presumably, they must have received some threats or perhaps some anonymous calls or had become aware that people had begun disappearing, that there were cases of arson, and they also heard of the persecution of population in the Japra valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you personally know persons who left before the takeover because of threats or anonymous calls or any of the matters you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not positive but I'm aware that the Ceric family left, I presume under pressure, and I know that they left the territory of Bosanski Novi. Then another family, Delic, and others.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Your Honour, that may be an appropriate moment nor a break because I'm going to move on to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you agree to 20 instead of the usual 25-minute break?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Unfortunately the interpreters cannot hear the Presiding Judge because the microphone was switched off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So 20 minute break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just reminded before we go on, I think we may have to go into private session for the description of what happened. That we've not had a decision on the protective measures motion for up and coming Novi witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So we do rather need that because we think we are going to move through the witnesses rather --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know that they are working on it. I have a meeting with Mr. Von hebel immediately after the sitting and I will see what stage they are at.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because, as I say, we anticipate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Gave a decision relating to a 92 bis witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think also with regard -- any way, I can't remember exactly what my instructions were. I'll check with Mr. Von hebel. I know that it's in the pipeline any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It can't stay in the pipeline much longer because we are going to be going through the witnesses fast. Your Honour, can I take it that we will sit through until 1.30 and then conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will sit right through to quarter to 2.00 but we may have to stop for two minutes to change the tapes. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to come, sir, to the night that -- of the takeover. Yes. I think we can wait for a moment before we go into private, unless we have gone in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not in private session as yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the night of the takeover you were actually at home. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the violence started, had anything alerted to you the fact that something might be going to happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing in particular, except that I did not notice a really normal situation. There were no people outside. Most houses were closed, and even though the weather was nice, it was a nice afternoon, but there was nobody out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I am now going to ask to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, Madam Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about the events after the takeover and I think we can use for, as it were, a starting point, a report that was made by the public security station in Bosanski Novi. Could you be handed, please, Exhibit 717?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is on the list so Your Honour should have copies there. And we need to go in it -- I think before it's handed to the witness, the usher better give it to me -- to the part that deals with Bosanski Novi. Your Honour, that's for our -- in the translation, it's quite a long document, it begins, Your Honour, at 00 -- 01109856. It's headed, "Bosanski Novi." I'll just try and find that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a report by the security services centre, Banja Luka, on the events in Bosanski Novi, and it was prepared on the 14th of August, 1992. And it says, "One, collection centres in Bosanski Novi municipality. Pursuant to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ministry of Defence decision of 16th of April, the decision of the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina in cooperation with the Bosanski Novi Territorial Defence municipal staff and representative of government organs, the public security station has prepared a plan to confiscate illegally acquired weapons." And so on and so forth. "The plan envisages the completion of these activities by 1500 hours on the 11th of May; however, with the voluntary surrender of weapons these activities did not produce the desired effect. And in addition, according to a report submitted by a military police patrol, they were attacked in the village of Blagaj Rijeka during the night of 10, 11 May. "As a result, a series of combat operations were directed against areas and villages with a majority Muslim population. Thus on the 24th of May, 1992, the entire population of the Japra valley villages was put up in the central part of the Blagaj Japra. After the burial of a member of the military police who had been killed during an attack on Prijedor, combat operations took place in the Prekosanje suburb on the evening of June 1992." Now, pausing there, please, sir, were you aware of the operations that had been conducted in the Japra valley? And you can just answer that yes or no because we are going to hear other evidence about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The description, as it's called, of the combat operations taking place in the Prekosanje suburb on the evening of the 1st of June, does that date, the 1st of June, correspond in your mind to what you were describing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that it was then when the power was taken over from the territory of Kula and hills above it, above that locality, fire was opened, and afterwards, I saw houses burning. The next day, I heard that there were also some fatalities in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That would seem to be what they are describing here. "All the combat operations mentioned above were carried out by armed uniformed men who were either self-organised or members of the Territorial Defence or JNA combat units and no members or policemen of the Bosanski Novi public security station took part in them. On 2nd of June, 1992, the forces of the Bosanski Novi Territorial Defence municipal staff and the military police began to round up non-Serbian citizens at the Mlakve stadium without the knowledge of or consultations with the Bosanski Novi public security station." All right. Now let's pause there. So did you become aware of people, non-Serbian citizens, being rounded up and put into the football stadium?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, and I listened to you carefully, the population in the Japra valley were the most populous, from the outskirts, from Gornji Agici to Donji Agici, Suhaca, Hozici, they were all evicted and brought to the territory of the village Blagaj Japra. They spent several days there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want -- as I say we are going to hear from other witnesses about that. I'm concerned now about the football stadium. Did you become aware of people --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. At that moment in time, they were not taken to the football stadium of the Sloboda club. They were brought back to the stadium. They were taken away and then brought back to the stadium.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's talk about the time when they were brought back to the stadium. What happened to them there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Other groups of citizens were also brought there apart from them, to this same stadium at Mlakve. Some estimates say that there were over 700 people who were put there and kept there for quite a long time, from the Japra valley, as far as I can remember, sometime in the second decade of May, were brought there, thus joining people who had already been brought to that stadium before them. As far as I know, there was -- there were some guards or rather the army was guarding them. They were fed, I don't know how regular the meals were, and from the conversation with Dr. Bokan I learned that, as the doctor told me, his duty was to go there, examine the sick, or extend the necessary aid at the Sloboda football stadium. They were not released before the 23rd of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that a doctor went there to treat them. Was he a Serb doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A Serb, yes, a Serb. I believe there were different doctors but this one was the one who went there most often, the Serbs always went there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the people who were kept there, were they men, women, and children, or were people separated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. From what I know, only men were at the stadium.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of these men get ill-treated by the people who were guarding them or by other people who were allowed in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, ill-treatment is a very broad term. They were -- there was offensive language, verbally abused too. According to Dr. Bokan, there were no drastic cases of ill-treatment apart from these abuses and insults, which were ethnically motivated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about provisions, food and drink and the like? Do you know whether that was provided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since the largest number of those men -- I mean, their families were not in the territory of the Bosanski Novi municipality, they had been sent in G-trains towards Doboj, that is one group was sent towards Maglaj, another one towards Batala [phoen] that is the area of Tuzla, and they were turned back, starting from men of younger age, to those very senior ones. They were brought back to the stadium of the Sloboda football club in Bosanski Novi from the Ostruznja station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, I just asking, do you know whether they were given -- the people who were being kept there, were they being given by their guards sufficient food and sufficient water and sanitary and bathing facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what I know, it was not enough what they got, because in -- you cannot find a reception centre where you're given enough food. But relatives, not male but female, from the territory of the town and the suburbs knew about the men who were kept there. And now and then the guards would allow those women to take food to persons incarcerated at the stadium.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you become aware of any other detention-type facilities within Bosanski Novi itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Bosanski Novi, individual arrests happened in the Una Hotel, that is in the discotheque, which was in the basement of the hotel. And I guess some rooms, too. And also the fire brigades house, that is the present cultural centre, which is on the bank of the Una in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that have a name, the fire brigade, which is now the cultural centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was built as the firemen's centre with all the necessary facilities. It was fully appointed as such. It had rooms. It had a hall, it had the depot for the engines, and also a storage space.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the Vatro -- I think I heard it through the interpretation -- the Vatrogasni Dom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It is on the bank of the Una itself, and according to what I know, and I've lived long in Bosanski Novi, it was called Vatrogasni Dom, that is the fireman's centre. Now it is both the cultural centre and the fireman's centre, that is Vatrogasni Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We better go into private session for just a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we go on back to this report, what happened to leaders of the Muslims in Bosanski Novi, that is leaders of the SDA and the like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a small explanation. The SDA leaders, yes, I knew them during the war. No contact except when I would run into them in the street. The President of the SDA, that is of the municipality of Bosanski Novi, I've already said that. For a while, he was in Bosanski Novi, then in time he left. And then he was killed. But the municipal board of the SDA, I knew some of them, not all of them -- or rather I didn't know they were members except Dzafer Kapetanovic, Misa Berberovic, and I think Ismet Muslimovic or Iso as we used to call him. They were arrested. They were taken -- they were first in the hotel, then they were taken elsewhere, perhaps the fireman's centre. Later on they were taken in an unknown direction and after torture and ill-treatment, and we still do not know their whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have they ever been seen since the end of the war in -- the end of the conflict in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They have not been seen. Now, in the wake of the war, they were not seen there. They were not seen in 1993, 1994, 1995. And to this day, and as likely as not, nobody will see them tomorrow either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we go back to the report that you were looking at? Because it carries on after dealing with the football stadium. "According to our information the municipal Territorial Defence staff resorted to this measure in order to put a stop to uncontrolled groups and units who not only carried out reprisals against the population but also took to destroying all premises and property owned by Muslim citizens. The people who were brought to the collection centre" -- this still refers I think to the football stadium -- "were not registered at this time but according to our information we assess that around 300 predominantly Muslim people were brought in. Most of them were men of military age, between 18 and 60, but there were also a few women and children, around 20 persons, from an area of the Prekosanje suburb which had been destroyed. The arrested persons were not processed by either the army or this public security station. The collection centre was dismantled on the 5th of June when most of the citizens were released and allowed to go home. A number of them, around 120 persons, voluntarily signed up to join wartime army units while a small number, some 17 people, who were considered to be of security interest, were detained on the premises of the military police. During their stay at the collection centre, the citizens had access to the football club sports and social facilities and they received water and food regularly." Now I want to come back to what they say about the release of these men, but I want to talk or ask you now about the description of the groups who were destroying premises and other property owned by Muslim citizens. After the takeover that you've described, at the beginning of June, what were the circumstances of what was happening in Bosanski Novi to the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I was also involved in that, that is as I also shared with others life in that town, I most emphatically say that the security service, and I mean what I'm saying when I say the "security service," I mean the police, in the public security station, that by and large did their job properly and tried to establish some order in the town. The units of the regular army at that time, and from what I know, were not involved in such activities, but I've already said that a group called dry ribs, "Suha Rebra," whose names are on record, they tortured, slaughtered, burned, forced people to jump off high storeys. I've already said that the security service did settle scores with that group. I know that because it happened near my house because I know that a member of that group, dry ribs, called Petic, was killed in front of the bank, and his brother was killed in front of the municipal hall. And the municipal hall what we call it, it was an Austrian building a long time ago, which is right next to the border with the Republic of Croatia, next to the bridge, and we called that building Veznica [phoen] which is the town hall or the municipal hall. There were also other groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So although the police, you say, tried to restore order, there were these groups going around and doing the actions that you've described, in particular the Suha Rebra?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But there were other groups too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what was the atmosphere like in the town of Bosanski Novi for those who were not Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The atmosphere in the early days, it was very tense, almost unbearable for a while, unbearable because apart from our safety being under threat -- the Bosniak corps, as a matter of fact, following the proclamation of some staff or other, the Bosniaks could not buy flour, edible oil, that is the basic necessities. And I also experienced that because I had some refugees in my house and some small children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there ever a refusal by shops in the town to serve or supply foodstuffs to non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not that it happened. They also had a piece of paper, and only some in some shops would show it, that Muslims were not allowed to buy flour and edible oil. I need to add that some Serbs, who had heard of the needs of their townsmen -- co-townsmen that they needed flour or oil or something, would meet them in the street and offer them help and they sometimes even would take flour or oil to their neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us about the Crisis Staff. Was Mr. Pasic the head of the Crisis Staff which declared itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the beginning, I think that Mr. Radomir Pasic discharged all the three offices, I think, the municipal mayor, the President of the Crisis Staff, and for a while, president of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Crisis Staff, during this period of time, during June of 1992, make announcements over the radio or other media?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The radio station aired certain provisions about the permissible conduct, what one is -- may or may not do, what happens in different parts of the town or outside it, so that we could all hear that. That is when we had electricity and when we could find the batteries for our transistor radios.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you allowed to move round the town freely and at any time? By "you," I mean you, the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a while, we could move around the town but I think that I think that the curfew covered a large part of the evening and night, when you couldn't move around. So we, the Bosniaks, did not go out, but I think that some other individuals, persons I believe of Serb ethnicity, could move about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did that curfew first start? Immediately after the events at the beginning of June, the takeover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In early June, I think, people imposed the curfew on themselves because the situation was so tense that one could never know when some armed group might turn up in a street, around the corner, and put your life in peril.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to move to the topic of the movement out of, as it's put in this report, citizens from Bosanski Novi. Can you go to the part of the report which says, "2, the moving out of citizens from Bosanski Novi municipality?"

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's at page 3 of that part of the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what it says there is, "After the adoption of the decision number," and it gives the number, "on the 4th of May, 1992, by the government of the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina, legal government organs initiated political activities to ensure that the necessary political and other measures and actions were taken to implement the decision to disarm." And it goes on to talk about disarming. Then it goes on to talk about the paramilitaries, and we've already dealt with that. And then it talks about the attacks on the villages. And on the 24th of May, the entire Muslim population leaving Blagaj, Japra. Now, if you go, please, to the part which begins, "According to an agreement with the representatives of the Bosanski Novi municipal assembly Crisis Staff." Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm looking at the document, moving out of the citizens from the territory, but that passage, no, I haven't found it -- yes, I have. "On the basis of the decision or following the decision." Is that it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It starts, "According to an agreement with the representatives of the Bosanski Novi municipal assembly Crisis Staff, on the 9th of June, 1992, the citizens from the Japra valley who were refugees in Blagaj Japra headed for Doboj in a railway train consists of 22 closed cars. In the assessment of a policeman working at this public security station who escorted the train from Blagaj to Doboj, around 4.000 people of all ages, male and female, boarded the train. The next day the 10th of June, 1992, 652 men fit for work were taken off the convoy in the Doboj area and returned to the municipality where, on instructions from the Crisis Staff, they were put up at the Mlakve collection centre." Now, were you aware of this train leaving and then people being returned to the football field, football centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for the relocation of people from the Japra valley, that is from Blagaj, yes, I was aware of that. I knew that they had been all put in freight cars. I suppose they were loaded on to these trains in Blagaj Rijeka, that is at the station itself, or perhaps in the area of what was it -- that is where the Japra company premises were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't worry about describing because, as I say, we are going to hear other evidence about that. Just -- but you were aware of that attempt to leave the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To leave, yes, but I emphatically say that it was people were not moving away of their own will. I mean, I do not think you can call voluntary departure when there is torture, when there are murders, when there are threats and so on, and most people had left their homes and houses to get there. So I would not really call it voluntary moving away or leaving, departure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We understand, sir. Now, can we just go on with this document? We see there, it says, if you move down the page, "Proceeding from a decision on the voluntary moving out of citizens issued by the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and an order by the Bosanski Novi municipality Crisis Staff on criteria for voluntary moving out, the Bosanski Novi public security station has, in accordance with due procedure, dealt with the citizens' requests in the following manner: Permanently cancelled the residency of 5.680 persons, issued certificates to 1.758, temporarily cancelled the residence of 41, and issued permits for temporary departure." And then it breaks it down. And then we see, "According to ethnicity, the total number of cancelled residencies was: Muslim, 5.629; Serbs, 3; Yugoslavs, 6; Croats, 2; Albanians, 38; Hungarians, 2." Then it goes on to say this: "In addition to a request for the permanent cancellation of residency, in accordance with the procedure prescribed by the existing laws and regulations, citizens who have moved out voluntarily have given written statements to the competent municipal organ that their moving was voluntary on the status of their moveable and immovable property and the routes by which they will leave and/or the places they wish to register or take up residence." And then it goes on to deal with the convoys which I want to finish up with. Now, what did people have to do before they were allowed to leave Bosanski Novi, the non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people who intended to leave, and I believe that it was the intention of almost the entire population to leave the area, well of course you have to stop mentioning voluntary, because it was not voluntary in any way, by any stretch of imagination.
